title.zh: 卷九十 烏桓鮮卑列傳
title.en: Volume 90: Treatise on the Wuhuan, Xianbei
title.raw: 卷九十 烏桓鮮卑列傳 Volume 90: Treatise on the Wuhuan, Xianbei

sentences.zh: 烏桓者，本東胡也。

translations.literal: The Wuhuan were, in origin, the Eastern Hu.
translations.idiomatic: The Wuhuan people were originally part of the Eastern Hu.

sentences.zh: 漢初，匈奴冒頓滅其國，餘類保烏桓山，因以為號焉。

translations.literal: At the beginning of the Han, the Xiongnu Modu destroyed their state; the remnant took refuge on Mount Wuhuan and thereby adopted it as their name.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Han dynasty, the Xiongnu ruler Modu wiped out their kingdom; those who survived sheltered on Mount Wuhuan and took that mountain's name as their own.

sentences.zh: 俗善騎射，弋獵禽獸為事。

translations.literal: By custom they were skilled at riding and archery; shooting and hunting birds and beasts was their occupation.
translations.idiomatic: They excelled at horsemanship and the bow, and made their living hunting birds and beasts.

sentences.zh: 隨水草放牧，居無常處。

translations.literal: They followed water and pasture in herding livestock; they dwelt without a fixed place.
translations.idiomatic: They moved their herds with grass and water and had no permanent homes.

sentences.zh: 以穹廬為舍，東開向日。

translations.literal: They took domed felt tents as dwellings, opening them toward the east to face the sun.
translations.idiomatic: They lived in round felt tents with the entrance facing east toward the sunrise.

sentences.zh: 食肉飲酪，以毛毳為衣。

translations.literal: They ate meat and drank kumis; they took wool and fine fur as clothing.
translations.idiomatic: Their diet was meat and fermented milk; they wore woolens and soft furs.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕貴少而賤老，其性悍塞。

translations.literal: [1] They honored the young and slighted the old; their nature was fierce and obstructive.
translations.idiomatic: [1] They esteemed youth and looked down on age; their temper ran fierce and stubborn.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕怒則殺父兄，而終不害其母，以母有族類，父兄無相仇報故也。

translations.literal: [2] In wrath they might kill father or elder brother, yet would never harm the mother, because the mother had a clan while father and elder brother had no reciprocal feud by which to be avenged.
translations.idiomatic: [2] They might kill a father or elder brother in anger, but never harmed the mother—she had her own kin who would answer for her, whereas no such obligation hung over patricide or fratricide.

sentences.zh: 有勇健能理決鬥訟者，推為大人，無世業相繼。

translations.literal: Whoever was brave, strong, and able to settle fights and lawsuits was pushed forward as a great man; there was no hereditary succession.
translations.idiomatic: Men who were courageous, robust, and could settle quarrels and legal disputes became "great men"; the office did not pass down through families.

sentences.zh: 邑落各有小帥，數百千落自為一部。

translations.literal: Each settlement had its petty chief; several hundred or a thousand settlements formed one tribe.
translations.idiomatic: Every camp had a minor leader, and hundreds or thousands of camps made up a single tribal division.

sentences.zh: 大人有所召呼，則刻木為信，雖無文字，而部眾不敢違犯。

translations.literal: When a great man summoned them, he carved wood as a token of trust; though they had no writing, the tribesmen did not dare disobey.
translations.idiomatic: A great man's summons was signaled by notched wood; without a written script, the people still never dared defy it.

sentences.zh: 氏姓無常，以大人健者名字為姓。

translations.literal: Clan surnames were not fixed; they took the personal names of vigorous great men as surnames.
translations.idiomatic: Surnames were not fixed; they often adopted the given names of renowned great men as clan names.

sentences.zh: 大人以下，各自畜牧營產，不相傜役。

translations.literal: Below the rank of great man, each pastured livestock and managed property on his own, without mutual corvée.
translations.idiomatic: Below the great men, everyone herded and earned his own keep, and none owed forced labor to another.

sentences.zh: 其嫁娶則先略女通情，〔三〕或半歲百日，然後送牛馬羊畜，以為娉幣。

translations.literal: In marriage they first abducted the girl to communicate affection; [3] sometimes after half a year or a hundred days they then sent cattle, horses, sheep, and livestock as bride-price.
translations.idiomatic: Courtship began with carrying off the bride-to-be to cement affection; [3] only after months—or a hundred days—did the groom's side deliver cattle, horses, and sheep as betrothal gifts.

sentences.zh: 婿隨妻還家，妻家無尊卑，旦旦拜之，而不拜其父母。

translations.literal: The groom followed the wife to her family's home; toward her family there was no distinction of seniority—each morning he bowed to them—but he did not bow to her parents.
translations.idiomatic: The husband moved in with his wife's people; he bowed every morning to everyone in her household without regard to rank, yet did not bow to her parents specifically.

sentences.zh: 為妻家僕役，一二年閒，妻家乃厚遣送女，居處財物一皆為辦。

translations.literal: He served as a bondsman to the wife's family; within a year or two the wife's family then generously sent off the daughter, providing in full dwelling and goods.
translations.idiomatic: He labored for his in-laws for a year or two; then they sent the couple off handsomely, outfitting them with a home and everything they needed.

sentences.zh: 其俗妻後母，報寡

translations.literal: In their custom men took their stepmothers as wives and practiced levirate toward widowed
translations.idiomatic: By custom a son could marry his stepmother and take a widowed

sentences.zh: 〈女更〉

translations.literal: (Textual note: variant reading 女更 for 嫂 "sister-in-law.")
translations.idiomatic: (Commentary variant on the preceding graph.)

sentences.zh: ，死則歸其故夫。

translations.literal: sister-in-law; when she died she was returned to her former husband [for joint burial].
translations.idiomatic: Under levirate she joined that sister-in-law's place in the household; when she died she was buried again with her first husband.

sentences.zh: 計謀從用婦人，唯鬥戰之事乃自決之。

translations.literal: Plans and stratagems followed women's counsel; only in matters of fighting did they decide by themselves.
translations.idiomatic: Women shaped strategy and counsel; men reserved decisions about combat for themselves.

sentences.zh: 父子男女相對踞蹲。

translations.literal: Fathers and sons, men and women, sat squatting facing one another.
translations.idiomatic: Men and women, young and old, squatted facing one another when they gathered.

sentences.zh: 以髡頭為輕便。

translations.literal: They took shaved heads as convenient.
translations.idiomatic: They shaved their heads for practicality.

sentences.zh: 婦人至嫁時乃養髮，分為髻，著句決，飾以金碧，猶中國有簂步搖。

translations.literal: Women only let their hair grow at marriage; they divided it into chignons, wore goujue ornaments, and adorned themselves with gold and jasper—like the guibu yao in China.
translations.idiomatic: Women grew their hair only when they married, arranged it in buns, wore clasps called goujue, and set gold and bright stones in their hair—much like Chinese women's headframes and swaying buyao pins.

sentences.zh: 〔四〕婦人能刺韋作文繡，織氀毼。

translations.literal: [4] Women could stitch leather into patterned embroidery and weave liuhe cloth.
translations.idiomatic: [4] Women embroidered patterns into leather and wove coarse woolens.

sentences.zh: 〔五〕男子能作弓矢鞍勒，〔六〕鍛金鐵為兵器。

translations.literal: [5][6] Men could craft bows, arrows, saddles, and bridles; they forged gold and iron into weapons.
translations.idiomatic: [5][6] Men fashioned bows, arrows, saddles, and bits, and hammered bronze and iron into arms.

sentences.zh: 其土地宜穄及東牆。

translations.literal: Their land was suited to broomcorn millet and dongqiang.
translations.idiomatic: Their soil grew broomcorn millet and a grain called dongqiang.

sentences.zh: 東牆似蓬草，實如穄子，至十月而熟。

translations.literal: Dongqiang resembled tumbleweed grass; its grain was like millet seed; it ripened by the tenth month.
translations.idiomatic: Dongqiang looked like wormwood, bore seeds like millet, and ripened in late autumn.

sentences.zh: 見鳥獸孕乳，以別四節。

translations.literal: Observing birds and beasts conceive and nurse their young, they distinguished the four seasons.
translations.idiomatic: They told the seasons by watching when animals bred and nursed their young.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 鄭玄注周禮曰：「毛之縟細者為毳也。」

translations.literal: [1] Zheng Xuan's commentary on the Rites of Zhou states: "What is fine and thin among fur is called cui."
translations.idiomatic: [1] Zheng Xuan glosses the Zhouli: the finest, softest animal hair is called cui.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 說文曰：「悍，勇也。

translations.literal: [2] The Shuowen jiezi says: "Han means brave."
translations.idiomatic: [2] The Shuowen glosses han as "courageous."

sentences.zh: 」塞謂不通。

translations.literal: " Sai means blocked and not open.
translations.idiomatic: As for sai in the compound glossed above, it means blocked and impervious, shut off from persuasion.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 杜預注左傳曰：「不以道取為略。」

translations.literal: [3] Du Yu's commentary on the Zuo zhuan says: "To take not by the proper way is lue, abduction."
translations.idiomatic: [3] Du Yu on the Zuo: seizing a woman without proper rites is lue, "carrying off."

sentences.zh: 〔四〕 簂音

translations.literal: [4] The character gui is read
translations.idiomatic: [4] Gui (head-dress) is pronounced

translations.literal: (ji).
translations.idiomatic: like "ji."

sentences.zh: 〔古〕誨反。

translations.literal: [ancient] hui fan (reverse cut).
translations.idiomatic: Using the fanqie spelling with initial hui (ancient gloss form).

sentences.zh: 字或為「幗」，婦人首飾也。

translations.literal: The graph may also be written 幗; it is women's head ornament.
translations.idiomatic: Other editions write the word as 幗—a woman's hairpiece.

sentences.zh: 續漢輿服志曰：「公卿列侯夫人紺繒幗。

translations.literal: The Xu Han treatise on coaches and dress says: "The wives of dukes, ministers, and ranked marquises wear dark silk gui."
translations.idiomatic: The Later Han dress code notes that noblewives bound their hair in dark silk gui caps.

sentences.zh: 」釋名云「皇后首飾，上有垂珠，步則搖之」也。

translations.literal: " The Shiming states: "The empress's head ornament bears pendant pearls that sway as she walks."
translations.idiomatic: The Shiming compares such adornment to the empress's pearls that trembled with each step.

sentences.zh: 〔五〕 廣雅曰：「氀毼，罽也。

translations.literal: [5] The Guangya says: "Liuhe is ji, felted wool."
translations.idiomatic: [5] The Guangya glosses liuhe as ji, a wool felt.

sentences.zh: 」氀音力于反。

translations.literal: " Liu is read li-yu fan (reverse cut).
translations.idiomatic: The syllable liu is spelled li-yu in fanqie notation.

sentences.zh: 毼音胡達反。

translations.literal: He is read hu-da fan.
translations.idiomatic: He takes the hu-da fanqie reading.

sentences.zh: 〔六〕 勒，馬銜也。

translations.literal: [6] Le means the horse bit.
translations.idiomatic: [6] Here le denotes the metal bit in a horse's mouth.

sentences.zh: 俗貴兵死，斂屍以棺，有哭泣之哀，至葬則歌舞相送。

translations.literal: By custom they honored dying in war; they gathered the corpse in a coffin and had the grief of weeping; when it came to burial they sang and danced to send one another off.
translations.idiomatic: They esteemed death in battle; kin laid out the body in a coffin and wept, then saw the dead away with song and dance.

sentences.zh: 肥養一犬，以彩繩纓牽，并取死者所乘馬衣物，皆燒而送之，言以屬累犬〔一〕，使護死者神靈歸赤山。

translations.literal: They fattened one dog, led it with a colored cord halter, and together took the horse and clothing the dead had ridden and worn, all burning them as send-off, saying thereby to entrust to the dog [1], making it escort the dead person's spirit to Mount Chi.
translations.idiomatic: They fattened a dog on a ribbon leash, burned its master's horse and garments with it, and meant by this entrustment [1] for the dog to guide the soul to Red Mountain.

sentences.zh: 赤山在遼東西北數千里，如中國人死者魂神歸岱山也。

translations.literal: Mount Chi lies several thousand li northwest of Liaodong; it is as when Chinese dead—their souls return to Mount Dai.
translations.idiomatic: Red Mountain stood thousands of li northwest of Liaodong—their counterpart to Mount Tai, where Chinese believed the dead returned.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕敬鬼神，祠天地日月星辰山川及先大人有健名者。

translations.literal: [2] They revered ghosts and spirits, sacrificing to Heaven and Earth, sun and moon, stars and constellations, mountains and rivers, and to former great men who had had worthy reputations.
translations.idiomatic: [2] They feared and honored spirits, offering to heaven and earth, the luminaries, mountains and rivers, and to mighty ancestors whose names lived on.

sentences.zh: 祠用牛羊，畢皆燒之。

translations.literal: For sacrifice they used cattle and sheep; when finished they burned them all.
translations.idiomatic: Oxen and sheep fed the altars, then the offerings went up in flame.

sentences.zh: 其約法：違大人言者，罪至死；

translations.literal: Their compact laws: whoever disobeyed a great man's words was guilty to the point of death.
translations.idiomatic: Their laws were blunt: defy a great man and you faced execution.

sentences.zh: 若相賊殺者，令部落自相報，不止，詣大人告之，聽出馬牛羊以贖死；

translations.literal: If parties slew one another in mutual injury, they ordered the tribes to avenge themselves among themselves; if it did not stop, they went to the great man to report it; he allowed producing horses, cattle, and sheep to ransom a death.
translations.idiomatic: Bloodletting between families was left to tribal vengeance first; if feuding continued, the great man stepped in and accepted livestock as weregild.

sentences.zh: 其自殺父兄則無罪；

translations.literal: But if one killed one's own father or elder brother there was no crime.
translations.idiomatic: Yet killing one's own father or brother carried no penalty.

sentences.zh: 若亡畔為大人所捕者，邑落不得受之，皆徙逐於雍狂之地，沙漠之中。

translations.literal: If one fled rebellion and was captured by a great man, the settlements might not receive him—all were relocated and driven to the Yongkuang lands, amid the desert.
translations.idiomatic: Deserters seized by a great man found no shelter in any camp and were herded into the wastes called Yongkuang.

sentences.zh: 其土多蝮蛇，在丁令西南，烏孫東北焉。

translations.literal: That soil had many pit vipers; it lay southwest of the Dingling and northeast of the Wusun.
translations.idiomatic: That desert swarmed with vipers, southwest of the Dingling and northeast of the Wusun.
[3] (End of commentary note.)

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 屬累猶付託也。

translations.literal: [1] Shulei means entrusting.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Shulei means handing something over in trust.

sentences.zh: 屬音之欲反。

translations.literal: Shu is read zhi-yu fan.
translations.idiomatic: Shu is read by the zhi-yu fanqie.

sentences.zh: 累音力瑞反。

translations.literal: Lei is read li-rui fan.
translations.idiomatic: Lei uses the li-rui fanqie.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 博物志：「泰山，天帝孫也，主召人魂。

translations.literal: [2] The Bowu zhi: "Mount Tai is the grandson of the Heaven Emperor; it presides at summoning men's souls.
translations.idiomatic: [2] Zhang Hua's Miscellanea says Mount Tai, grandson of heaven, gathers wandering souls.

sentences.zh: 東方萬物始，故知人生命。」

translations.literal: In the east the myriad things begin; therefore it knows the span of human life."
translations.idiomatic: Because life springs from the east, the mountain knows each mortal's allotted years."

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 前書音義曰：「丁令，匈奴別種也。

translations.literal: [3] The Former Han shu yinyi says: "The Dingling are a separate stock of the Xiongnu.
translations.idiomatic: [3] The Former Han pronunciation gloss calls the Dingling a Xiongnu offshoot.

sentences.zh: 令音零。」

translations.literal: Ling is read ling."
translations.idiomatic: The syllable ling rhymes with "zero" (ling)."

sentences.zh: 烏桓自為冒頓所破，眾遂孤弱，常臣伏匈奴，歲輸牛馬羊皮，過時不具，輒沒其妻子。

translations.literal: From the time the Wuhuan were broken by Modu, their masses became isolated and weak; they regularly submitted as vassals to the Xiongnu, yearly delivering cattle, horses, and sheep hides—if past due they were not complete, then their wives and children were seized.
translations.idiomatic: After Modu shattered them, the Wuhuan remained few and dependent, yearly paying the Xiongnu in livestock and hides; late tribute meant forfeiture of wives and children.

sentences.zh: 及武帝遣驃騎將軍霍去病擊破匈奴左地，因徙烏桓於上谷、漁陽、右北平、遼西、遼東五郡塞外，為漢偵察匈奴動靜。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu sent General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry Huo Qubing to crush the Xiongnu left wing, he therefore relocated the Wuhuan beyond the passes of Shanggu, Yuyang, Youbeiping, Liaoxi, and Liaodong to spy on Xiongnu movements for Han.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu had Huo Qubing break the left wing of the Xiongnu, then resettled the Wuhuan outside five northern commanderies so they could watch the steppe for Han.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕其大人歲一朝見，於是始置護烏桓校尉，秩二千石，擁節監領之，使不得與匈奴交通。

translations.literal: [1] Their great men had an annual audience; thereupon was first established the Colonel Protecting the Wuhuan, salary grade two thousand shi, bearing credentials to supervise and command them, causing them not to communicate with the Xiongnu.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Tribal leaders presented yearly tribute at court, and Han created the Colonel Protecting the Wuhuan—a full two-thousand-shi post with imperial credentials—to keep them from dealing with the Xiongnu.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 偵，覘也，音丑政反。

translations.literal: [1] Zhen means chan, spy; read chou-zheng fan.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Zhen means to reconnoiter; the gloss gives the chou-zheng fanqie pronunciation.

sentences.zh: 昭帝時，烏桓漸強，乃發匈奴單于冢墓，以報冒頓之怨。

translations.literal: In Emperor Zhao's time the Wuhuan gradually grew strong; they then dug open the tombs of Xiongnu chanyus to repay Modu's old wrong.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Zhao the Wuhuan grew bold enough to open Xiongnu royal tombs, striking back at Modu's ancient destruction of their kingdom.

sentences.zh: 匈奴大怒，乃東擊破烏桓。

translations.literal: The Xiongnu were greatly angered and thereupon struck east and defeated the Wuhuan.
translations.idiomatic: Enraged, the Xiongnu swept east and shattered the Wuhuan hosts.

sentences.zh: 大將軍霍光聞之，因遣度遼將軍范明友將二萬騎出遼東邀匈奴，而虜已引去。

translations.literal: Grand General Huo Guang heard of it and therefore sent General Who Crosses the Liao Fan Mingyou with twenty thousand horse east from Liaodong to intercept the Xiongnu, but the barbarians had already withdrawn.
translations.idiomatic: Huo Guang ordered Fan Mingyou and twenty thousand cavalry toward Liaodong to cut off the Xiongnu—who had already slipped away.

sentences.zh: 明友乘烏桓新敗，遂進擊之，斬首六千餘級，獲其三王首而還。

translations.literal: Mingyou took advantage of the Wuhuan's fresh defeat, then advanced and attacked them, beheading more than six thousand grades and capturing the heads of three kings before returning.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Mingyou turned on the beaten Wuhuan, claimed six thousand heads, and brought back three kings' skulls.

sentences.zh: 由是烏桓復寇幽州，明友輒破之。

translations.literal: Thereupon the Wuhuan again raided Youzhou; Mingyou regularly defeated them.
translations.idiomatic: The Wuhuan struck Youzhou again and again; Fan Mingyou drove them back each time.

sentences.zh: 宣帝時，乃稍保塞降附。

translations.literal: In Emperor Xuan's time they then gradually guarded the passes and submitted.
translations.idiomatic: By Emperor Xuan's reign they had begun to settle along the frontier and accept Han overlordship.

sentences.zh: 及王莽篡位，欲擊匈奴，興十二部軍，使東域將嚴尤領烏桓、丁令兵屯代郡，皆質其妻子於郡縣。

translations.literal: When Wang Mang usurped the throne, wishing to strike the Xiongnu he raised twelve army divisions, ordered General of the Eastern Regions Yan You to lead Wuhuan and Dingling troops garrisoned in Dai commandery, and all lodged their wives and children as hostages in the commanderies and counties.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Mang mobilized twelve armies against the Xiongnu and put Yan You in charge of Wuhuan and Dingling auxiliaries in Dai, holding every man's family hostage in county towns.

sentences.zh: 烏桓不便水土，懼久屯不休，數求謁去。

translations.literal: The Wuhuan did not acclimate to water and soil; they feared long encampment without end and repeatedly begged leave to depart.
translations.idiomatic: Unsuited to the climate and dreading endless service, they repeatedly petitioned to go home.

sentences.zh: 莽不肯遣，遂自亡畔，還為抄盜，而諸郡盡殺其質，由是結怨於莽。

translations.literal: Mang would not send them off; they therefore fled rebellion on their own, returning to raiding and banditry, while the commanderies all executed their hostages—thereby incurring enmity with Mang.
translations.idiomatic: Mang refused discharge, so they deserted and turned bandit; local officials slaughtered their hostages, and the tribes burned with hatred for Wang Mang.

sentences.zh: 匈奴因誘其豪帥以為吏，餘者皆羈縻屬之。

translations.literal: The Xiongnu thereupon enticed their heroic chiefs to become officials; the remainder were all loosely tethered and attached to them.
translations.idiomatic: The Xiongnu won over Wuhuan headmen with offices and kept the rest on a loose leash.

sentences.zh: 光武初，烏桓與匈奴連兵為寇，代郡以東尤被其害。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Guangwu, the Wuhuan joined arms with the Xiongnu as raiders; east of Dai commandery they especially suffered harm.
translations.idiomatic: Early in Emperor Guangwu's reign Wuhuan and Xiongnu horsemen struck together, worst of all east of Dai.

sentences.zh: 居止近塞，朝發穹廬，暮至城郭，五郡民庶，家受其辜，至於郡縣損壞，百姓流亡。

translations.literal: Dwelling halted near the passes, setting out from domed tents at dawn they reached walled towns by dusk; the common people of the five commanderies, household by household, bore the injury of it, to the point that commanderies and counties were damaged and common people fled wandering.
translations.idiomatic: Camped beside the frontier, they could leave their tents at dawn and raid Chinese towns by nightfall; five northern commanderies were ruined household by household until counties collapsed and people fled.

sentences.zh: 其在上谷塞外白山者，最為強富。

translations.literal: Those who were beyond the Shanggu pass at White Mountain were the strongest and richest.
translations.idiomatic: The band beyond White Mountain outside Shanggu grew richest and fiercest.

sentences.zh: 建武二十一年，遣伏波將軍馬援將三千騎出五阮關掩擊之。

translations.literal: In Jianwu twenty-first year he sent General Who Calms the Waves Ma Yuan leading three thousand horse out Wuyuan Pass for a surprise strike on them.
translations.idiomatic: In CE 45 Emperor Guangwu sent Ma Yuan with three thousand cavalry through Wuyuan Pass against them.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕烏桓逆知，悉相率逃走，追斬百級而還。

translations.literal: [1] The Wuhuan learned beforehand; all led one another in flight; pursuing, they beheaded a hundred grades and returned.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Forewarned, the Wuhuan slipped away in a body; Han pursuit bagged only a hundred heads.

sentences.zh: 烏桓復尾擊援後，援遂晨夜奔歸，比入塞，馬死者千餘匹。

translations.literal: The Wuhuan again struck Ma Yuan's rear in trailing attack; Yuan therefore ran day and night homeward; by the time he entered the passes more than a thousand horses had died.
translations.idiomatic: They harried his retreat until he raced night and day for the frontier, losing more than a thousand mounts.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 關在代郡。

translations.literal: [1] The pass lies in Dai commandery.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Wuyuan Pass stood in Dai commandery.

sentences.zh: 二十二年，匈奴國亂，烏桓乘弱擊破之，匈奴轉北徙數千里，漠南地空，帝乃以幣帛賂烏桓。

translations.literal: Twenty-second year, the Xiongnu state was in turmoil; the Wuhuan took advantage of weakness and defeated them; the Xiongnu shifted north several thousand li and the south of the desert was empty; the emperor therefore used silk goods to bribe the Wuhuan.
translations.idiomatic: The next year civil war weakened the Xiongnu; the Wuhuan drove them northward and emptied the southern steppe, so Han bought Wuhuan loyalty with silk.

sentences.zh: 二十五年，遼西烏桓大人郝旦等九百二十二人率眾向化，詣闕朝貢，獻奴婢牛馬及弓虎豹貂皮。

translations.literal: Twenty-fifth year, Wuhuan great men of Liaoxi such as Hao Dan, nine hundred twenty-two persons, led the masses toward civilization, coming to the palace to court tribute, presenting slaves, cattle, horses, and bows, tiger, leopard, and sable pelts.
translations.idiomatic: In CE 49 nine hundred twenty-two Liaoxi notables led by Hao Dan came to court with tribute—slaves, livestock, bows, and fine furs.

sentences.zh: 是時四夷朝賀，絡驛而至，天子乃命大會勞饗，賜以珍寶。

translations.literal: At this time the four barbarians came to court in congratulation, arriving in relays; the Son of Heaven therefore ordered a great assembly to feast and reward them, bestowing precious treasures.
translations.idiomatic: Frontier peoples were arriving in streams for audience; the emperor held a grand banquet and showered them with gifts.

sentences.zh: 烏桓或願留宿衛，於是封其渠帥為侯王君長者八十一人，皆居塞內，布於緣邊諸郡，令招來種人，給其衣食，遂為漢偵候，助擊匈奴、鮮卑。

translations.literal: Some Wuhuan wished to remain as palace guards; thereupon he enfeoffed eighty-one of their channel chiefs as marquises, kings, or lord elders; all dwelt inside the passes, spread along the frontier commanderies, ordered to summon their kindred, supplying them clothing and food—thereby becoming Han scouts assisting in striking the Xiongnu and Xianbei.
translations.idiomatic: Those who volunteered for imperial guard duty earned titles for eighty-one chiefs; Han settled them inside the wall along the border, fed and clothed them, and used them as scouts against Xiongnu and Xianbei.

sentences.zh: 時司徒掾班彪上言：「烏桓天性輕黠，好為寇賊，若久放縱而無總領者，必復侵掠居人，但委主降掾史，〔一〕恐非所能制。

translations.literal: At the time Steward Clerk of the Minister of Education Ban Biao submitted words: "The Wuhuan by nature are light and crafty, fond of acting as bandits; if long indulged without an overall leader, they will surely again invade and plunder settled people—merely entrusting chief clerks for surrender affairs [1], I fear it will not be possible to control them.
translations.idiomatic: Ban Biao warned the throne: "The Wuhuan are restless and predatory; leave them without a strong overseer and they will plunder Chinese settlers again—clerks who handle surrenders alone cannot hold them in check."

sentences.zh: 臣愚以為宜復置烏桓校尉，誠有益於附集，省國家之邊慮。

translations.literal: Your foolish servant thinks it fitting again to establish the Colonel of the Wuhuan; truly there is benefit in gathering attachment and sparing the state's frontier worries.
translations.idiomatic: This humble official urges restoring the Colonel Protecting the Wuhuan—it would win their loyalty and spare the frontier endless anxiety."

sentences.zh: 」帝從之。

translations.literal: " The emperor followed it.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor agreed.

sentences.zh: 於是始復置校尉於上谷甯城，〔二〕開營府，并領鮮卑，賞賜質子，歲時互市焉。

translations.literal: Thereupon he first again placed the colonel at Ningcheng in Shanggu; [2] opened camp headquarters, concurrently commanding the Xianbei, conferring rewards on hostages, and holding mutual markets by season.
translations.idiomatic: Han reopened the colonel's headquarters at Ningcheng in Shanggu, [2] added Xianbei to his brief, paid stipends to noble hostages, and ran seasonal border markets.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 蓋當時權置也。

translations.literal: [1] Presumably it was a provisional appointment of that time.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Those clerks were only ad hoc officers.

sentences.zh: 下兵馬掾亦同也。

translations.literal: The clerk below for horse and arms was likewise the same.
translations.idiomatic: The same applied to the horse-and-arms clerks.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 甯城，縣名。

translations.literal: [2] Ningcheng is a county name.
translations.idiomatic: [2] Ningcheng was a county seat.

sentences.zh: 前書甯縣作「寧」，史記甯城亦作「寧」，寧甯兩字通也。

translations.literal: The Former Han shu writes Ning county with the peace-character graph for ning; the Records of the Historian also writes Ningcheng with that same graph—the two variant ning graphs interchange.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier histories spell the county with the peace-character ning; an alternate graph was also read ning, and editors treated the two spellings as equivalent.

sentences.zh: 及明、章、和三世，皆保塞無事。

translations.literal: Through the three reigns of Ming, Zhang, and He, all guarded the passes without incident.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperors Ming, Zhang, and He the frontier stayed quiet.

sentences.zh: 安帝永初三年夏，漁陽烏桓與右北平胡千餘寇代郡、上谷。

translations.literal: Summer of Emperor An's Yongchu third year, Yuyang Wuhuan and over a thousand Hu of Youbeiping raided Dai commandery and Shanggu.
translations.idiomatic: In the summer of CE 109 Yuyang Wuhuan joined more than a thousand Youbeiping tribesmen to raid Dai and Shanggu.

sentences.zh: 秋，鴈門烏桓率眾王無何

translations.literal: Autumn, Yanmen Wuhuan leader-of-the-masses king Wuhe
translations.idiomatic: That autumn the Yanmen Wuhuan king Wuhe

translations.literal: (variant reading yun).
translations.idiomatic: (Some texts read the second graph as 允.)

sentences.zh: ，與鮮卑大人丘倫等，及南匈奴骨都侯，合七千騎寇五原，與太守戰於九原高渠谷，〔一〕漢兵大敗，殺郡長吏。

translations.literal: He joined Xianbei great men such as Qiulun and the Southern Xiongnu Gutu marquis; seven thousand riders together raided Wuyuan and fought the grand warden at Jiuyuan Gaqu Valley; [1] Han troops suffered a crushing defeat and the raiders slew the commandery's ranking officers.
translations.idiomatic: Wuhe then allied with Qiulun's Xianbei and the Southern Xiongnu Gutu marquis—seven thousand horsemen struck Wuyuan. At Gaqu Valley near Jiuyuan they routed Han troops and killed the chief county officers.

sentences.zh: 乃遣車騎將軍何熙、度遼將軍梁慬等擊，大破之。

translations.literal: Thereupon he sent General of Chariots and Cavalry He Xi, General Who Crosses the Liao Liang Jin, and others to strike them; greatly defeated them.
translations.idiomatic: Court dispatched He Xi and Liang Jin; they crushed the coalition.

sentences.zh: 無何乞降，鮮卑走還塞外。

translations.literal: Wuhe begged surrender; the Xianbei ran back beyond the passes.
translations.idiomatic: Wuhe capitulated and the Xianbei fled beyond the frontier.

sentences.zh: 是後烏桓稍復親附，拜其大人戎朱廆為親漢都尉。

translations.literal: After this the Wuhuan gradually drew close to Han again; the court invested their great man Rong Zhuwei as Commander Close to Han.
translations.idiomatic: The Wuhuan soon edged back toward friendship with Han, and the emperor named their chieftain Rong Zhuwei “Commander Close to Han.”
[2] (End of note.)

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 九原，縣名，屬五原郡。

translations.literal: [1] Jiuyuan is the name of a county in Wuyuan commandery.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Jiuyuan county lay in Wuyuan commandery.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 廆音胡罪反。

translations.literal: [2] The graph wei is read with the hu-zui fanqie spelling.
translations.idiomatic: [2] Wei is pronounced per the hu-zui fanqie gloss.

sentences.zh: 順帝陽嘉四年冬，烏桓寇雲中，遮截道上商賈車牛千餘兩，度遼將軍耿曄率二千餘人追擊，不利，又戰於沙南，斬首五百級。

translations.literal: In the winter of Emperor Shun’s fourth Yangjia year the Wuhuan raided Yunzhong, cutting off more than a thousand merchant carts and ox teams on the road; General Who Crosses the Liao Geng Ye pursued with over two thousand men without success, fought again south of Sha, and took five hundred heads.
translations.idiomatic: That winter Wuhuan riders plundered Yunzhong and ambushed a long wagon train of traders; Geng Ye chased them with two thousand troops, missed his first chance, then fought south of Sha County and claimed five hundred kills.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕烏桓遂圍曄於蘭池城，於是發積射士二千人，度遼營千人，配上郡屯，以討烏桓，烏桓乃退。

translations.literal: [1] The Wuhuan then besieged Ye at Lancheng; the court sent two thousand crack archers, a thousand men from the Liao garrison, and Shang commandery militia against them, and the Wuhuan withdrew.
translations.idiomatic: [1] They trapped Geng Ye in Lancheng until Han rushed archers, frontier troops, and Shang commandery reserves—the raiders then melted away.

sentences.zh: 永和五年，烏桓大人阿堅、羌渠等與南匈奴左部句龍吾斯反畔，中郎將張耽擊破斬之，餘眾悉降。

translations.literal: In the fifth Yonghe year Wuhuan leaders A Jian and Qiang Qu joined the Southern Xiongnu left-wing chief Goulong Wusi in revolt; Chief Commander Zhang Dan crushed the rebels and executed the ringleaders, and the rest surrendered.
translations.idiomatic: Yonghe 140: Wuhuan chiefs and Southern Xiongnu mutineers rose together; Zhang Dan broke them, beheaded the leaders, and accepted the survivors’ surrender.

sentences.zh: 桓帝永壽中，朔方烏桓與休著屠各並畔，中郎將張奐搫平之。

translations.literal: During Emperor Huan’s Yongshou era Shuofang Wuhuan and the Xiuzhu Tuge band rebelled together; Chief Commander Zhang Huan stamped out the rising.
translations.idiomatic: Mid-reign of Emperor Huan, Shuofang Wuhuan and Tuge auxiliaries mutinied; Zhang Huan flattened them.

sentences.zh: 延熹九年夏，烏桓復與鮮卑及南匈奴

translations.literal: In the summer of the ninth Yanxi year the Wuhuan again joined with the Xianbei and the Southern Xiongnu
translations.idiomatic: In the summer of Yanxi 166 (166 CE) the Wuhuan again allied with the Xianbei and the Southern Xiongnu

sentences.zh: （鮮卑）

translations.literal: (Textual gloss: “Xianbei.”)
translations.idiomatic: (Some manuscripts repeat the name “Xianbei” here.)

sentences.zh: 寇緣邊九郡，俱反，張奐討之，皆出塞去。

translations.literal: They raided nine frontier commanderies together in rebellion; Zhang Huan campaigned against them and they fled beyond the passes.
translations.idiomatic: Together they struck nine border prefectures in revolt. Zhang Huan drove every band back across the frontier.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 沙南，縣，屬雲中郡，有蘭池城。

translations.literal: [1] Shanan is a county of Yunzhong commandery and contains Lancheng.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Shanan County in Yunzhong held the fortress at Lancheng.

sentences.zh: 靈帝初，烏桓大人上谷有難樓者，眾九千餘落，遼西有丘力居者，眾五千餘落，皆自稱王；

translations.literal: Early in Emperor Ling’s reign the Shanggu Wuhuan chief Nanlou commanded more than nine thousand camps, while Liaoxi’s Qiuliju had over five thousand; each styled himself king.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Ling, Nanlou of Shanggu ruled nine thousand camps and Qiuliju of Liaoxi five thousand; both called themselves kings.

sentences.zh: 又遼東蘇僕延，眾千餘落，自稱峭王〔一〕；

translations.literal: Supuyan of Liaodong had more than a thousand camps and called himself the Precipice King, note one.
translations.idiomatic: Supuyan in Liaodong led a thousand camps and styled himself the Precipice King; see commentary note one on the pronunciation.

sentences.zh: 右北平烏延，眾八百餘落，自稱汗魯王：並勇建而多計策。

translations.literal: Wuyan of Youbeiping had more than eight hundred camps and called himself the Khan-Lu king; together they were fierce, capable fighters full of stratagems.
translations.idiomatic: Youbeiping’s Wuyan led eight hundred camps as “Khan-Lu king.” All four were bold warlords and shrewd planners.

sentences.zh: 中平四年，前中山太守張純畔，入丘力居眾中，自號彌天安定王，遂為諸郡烏桓元帥，寇掠青、徐、幽、冀四州。

translations.literal: In the fourth Zhongping year the former Zhongshan grand warden Zhang Chun rebelled, entered Qiuliju’s host, proclaimed himself the king who would “pacify heaven and stabilize all,” and became commander-in-chief of the frontier Wuhuan, pillaging Qing, Xu, You, and Ji.
translations.idiomatic: Zhongping 187: ex-magistrate Zhang Chun defected to Qiuliju, crowned himself a messianic war-king, and led Wuhuan bands across four provinces.

sentences.zh: 五年，以劉虞為幽州牧，虞購募斬純首，北州乃定。

translations.literal: The next year Liu Yu was appointed governor of Youzhou; he posted rewards, someone delivered Zhang Chun’s head, and the north grew quiet again.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Yu took Youzhou, put a price on Zhang Chun’s head, and peace returned to the northern commanderies.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 峭音七笑反。

translations.literal: [1] Qiao is read with the qi-xiao fanqie spelling.
translations.idiomatic: [1] “Precipice” (qiao) uses the qi-xiao fanqie reading.

sentences.zh: 獻帝初平中，丘力居死，子樓班年少，從子蹋頓有武略，代立，〔一〕總攝三郡，眾皆從其號令。

translations.literal: During Emperor Xian’s Chuping era Qiuliju died; his son Louban was still a boy, but his nephew Tadun was a seasoned commander and succeeded him [1], controlling three commanderies while everyone obeyed his orders.
translations.idiomatic: After Qiuliju died, young Louban yielded leadership to his cousin Tadun [1], who united three Wuhuan divisions under one voice.

sentences.zh: 建安初，冀州牧袁紹與前將軍公孫瓚相持不決，蹋頓遣使詣紹求和親，遂遣兵助擊瓚，破之。

translations.literal: Early in the Jian’an era Ji Province Governor Yuan Shao and former general Gongsun Zan were deadlocked; Tadun sent envoys seeking alliance with Shao, then sent troops that helped defeat Zan.
translations.idiomatic: As Yuan Shao and Gongsun Zan exhausted each other, Tadun offered Yuan Shao an alliance and auxiliaries that tipped the war.

sentences.zh: 紹矯制賜蹋頓、難樓、蘇僕延、烏延等，皆以單于印綬。

translations.literal: Shao forged an imperial writ granting Tadun, Nanlou, Supuyan, Wuyan, and others chanyu seals and ribbons.
translations.idiomatic: Yuan Shao counterfeited an edict and handed out chanyu regalia to every major Wuhuan chief.

sentences.zh: 後難樓、蘇僕延率其部眾奉樓班為單于，蹋頓為王，然蹋頓猶秉計策。

translations.literal: Later Nanlou and Supuyan elevated Louban as chanyu and Tadun as “king,” yet Tadun still held real authority.
translations.idiomatic: The tribes later crowned Louban chanyu and named Tadun “king,” but strategy stayed Tadun’s.

sentences.zh: 廣陽人閻柔，少沒烏桓、鮮卑中，為其種人所歸信，柔乃因鮮卑眾，殺烏桓校尉邢舉而代之。

translations.literal: Yan Rou of Guangyang had grown up a captive among Wuhuan and Xianbei and won their trust; he rallied Xianbei warriors, slew Colonel Xing Ju, and took the colonel’s office.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Rou, raised on the steppe, murdered Colonel Xing Ju with Xianbei support and claimed his post.

sentences.zh: 袁紹因寵慰柔，以安北邊。

translations.literal: Yuan Shao courted Rou to steady the northern frontier.
translations.idiomatic: Yuan Shao pampered Yan Rou to keep the border calm.

sentences.zh: 及紹子尚敗，奔蹋頓。

translations.literal: When Shao’s son Shang was beaten in the field, he fled to Tadun.
translations.idiomatic: After Yuan Shang’s defeat he rode to Tadun’s camps.

sentences.zh: 時幽、冀吏人奔烏桓者十萬餘戶，尚欲憑其兵力，復圖中國。

translations.literal: More than a hundred thousand households of You and Ji refugees lived under Wuhuan protection; Shang hoped to use their strength to strike back into the Central Plain.
translations.idiomatic: A hundred thousand Han households had fled north; Yuan Shang meant to lever their warriors for another grab at the heartland.

sentences.zh: 會曹操平河北，閻柔率鮮卑、烏桓歸附，操即以柔為校尉。

translations.literal: Once Cao Cao pacified Hebei, Yan Rou brought Xianbei and Wuhuan over to Han; Cao immediately confirmed him as colonel.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao’s victory drew Yan Rou in with Xianbei and Wuhuan auxiliaries, and Cao kept him as colonel.

sentences.zh: 建安十二年，曹操自征烏桓，大破蹋頓於柳城，斬之，首虜二十餘萬人。

translations.literal: In Jian’an 207 Cao Cao personally campaigned against the Wuhuan, shattered Tadun at Liucheng, executed him, and counted over two hundred thousand captives and heads.
translations.idiomatic: Jian’an 12: Cao Cao marched north, broke Tadun at Liucheng, took his head, and claimed two hundred thousand prisoners and casualties.

sentences.zh: 袁尚與樓班、烏延等皆走遼東，遼東太守公孫康並斬送之。

translations.literal: Yuan Shang fled to Liaodong with Louban and Wuyan; Liaodong grand warden Gongsun Kang executed them all and forwarded the heads.
translations.idiomatic: Gongsun Kang killed Yuan Shang, Louban, Wuyan, and their escorts when they sought refuge in Liaodong.

sentences.zh: 其餘眾萬餘落，悉徙居中國云。

translations.literal: The more than ten thousand remaining camps were reportedly resettled inside China.
translations.idiomatic: More than ten thousand camps were afterward moved into Han territory, tradition says.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 蹋音大蠟反。

translations.literal: [1] Ta is read with the da-la fanqie spelling.
translations.idiomatic: [1] “Ta” in Tadun follows the da-la fanqie gloss.

sentences.zh: 鮮卑者，亦東胡之支也，別依鮮卑山，故因號焉。

translations.literal: The Xianbei were another Eastern Hu offshoot who took their name from Mount Xianbei, where they settled apart.
translations.idiomatic: The Xianbei were Eastern Hu kin who named themselves after Mount Xianbei.

sentences.zh: 其言語習俗與烏桓同。

translations.literal: Their speech and customs matched the Wuhuan.
translations.idiomatic: Language and lifestyle mirrored the Wuhuan.

sentences.zh: 唯婚姻先髡頭，以季春月大會於饒樂水上，〔一〕飲讌畢，然後配合。

translations.literal: Only in marriage did they first shave the head; on the last month of spring they gathered by the Raole River [1], feasted, and then paired off.
translations.idiomatic: They shaved before weddings and held a spring rendezvous on the Raole River [1]; after the banquet couples paired up.

sentences.zh: 又禽獸異於中國者，野馬、原羊、角端牛，以角為弓，俗謂之角端弓者。

translations.literal: Their beasts unlike China’s included wild horses, yuan sheep, and horn-nosed cattle; bows carved from those horns were called “horn-nose bows.”
translations.idiomatic: Steppe fauna included wild horses, stocky sheep, and horn-heavy cattle whose horns became the famed “horn-point” bows.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕又有貂、豽、鼲子，皮毛柔蝡，〔三〕故天下以為名裘。

translations.literal: [2] They also had sable, na beasts, and hun rodents—pelts so soft [3] that the realm prized them as premier furs.
translations.idiomatic: [2] Sable, na, and hun hides—remarkably supple [3]—were counted the empire’s finest furs.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 水在今營州北。

translations.literal: [1] That river lies north of modern Yingzhou.
translations.idiomatic: [1] The Raole River ran north of Tang-era Yingzhou.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 郭璞注爾雅曰：「原羊似吳羊而大角，出西方。

translations.literal: [2] Guo Pu’s Erya commentary says: “The yuan sheep resembles the Wu sheep but bears huge horns and comes from the west.
translations.idiomatic: [2] Guo Pu notes giant-horned “yuan sheep” from the western marches.

sentences.zh: 」前書音義曰：「角端似牛，角可為弓。」

translations.literal: ” The Former Han pronunciation gloss adds: “The horn-nose resembles cattle; its horn makes bows.”
translations.idiomatic: Earlier scholars describe “horn-point” cattle whose horns serve as bow staves.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 豽音女滑反。

translations.literal: [3] Na is read nü-hua fan.
translations.idiomatic: [3] Na uses the nü-hua fanqie.

sentences.zh: 鼲音胡昆反。

translations.literal: Hun is read hu-kun fan.
translations.idiomatic: Hun takes the hu-kun fanqie reading.

sentences.zh: 貂、鼲並鼠屬。

translations.literal: Sable and hun belong among the marmot-like rodents.
translations.idiomatic: Sable and hun are classified with burrowing rodents.

sentences.zh: 豽，猴屬也。

translations.literal: Na belongs among the monkeys.
translations.idiomatic: Na is grouped with monkey-like creatures.

sentences.zh: 漢初，亦為冒頓所破，遠竄遼東塞外，與烏桓相接，未常通中國焉。

translations.literal: Early in the Han they too had been shattered by Modu and driven deep beyond the Liaodong frontier beside the Wuhuan, without regular contact with China.
translations.idiomatic: Like the Wuhuan they fled Modu into the Liaodong wilds and seldom dealt with the interior court.

sentences.zh: 光武初，匈奴強盛，率鮮卑與烏桓寇抄北邊，殺略吏人，無有寧歲。

translations.literal: When Guangwu came to power the strong Xiongnu led Xianbei and Wuhuan raids that killed officials and civilians year after year.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Guangwu the Xiongnu marched Xianbei and Wuhuan allies against the north until no year stayed peaceful.

sentences.zh: 建武二十一年，鮮卑與匈奴入遼東，遼東太守祭肜擊破之，斬獲殆盡，事已具肜傳，由是震怖。

translations.literal: In Jianwu 21 Xianbei and Xiongnu entered Liaodong; grand warden Zhai Tong crushed them almost to the last man—the story fills his biography—and left them terrified.
translations.idiomatic: Zhai Tong’s Liaodong defense in Jianwu 21 nearly annihilated a joint Xianbei-Xiongnu thrust and broke their nerve; see his biography.

sentences.zh: 及南單于附漢，北虜孤弱，二十五年，鮮卑始通驛使。

translations.literal: After the Southern Chanyu submitted to Han the northern tribes weakened; in the twenty-fifth Jianwu year the Xianbei first sent envoys along the post roads.
translations.idiomatic: Southern submission drained the northern steppe; by Jianwu 49 Xianbei riders opened diplomatic traffic with Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 其後都護偏何等詣祭肜求自效功，因令擊北匈奴左伊育訾部，斬首二千餘級。

translations.literal: Protector-in-chief Pian He later begged Zhai Tong for a chance to prove loyalty and was aimed at the Northern Xiongnu left Wing Yuyuzi tribe, losing over two thousand heads.
translations.idiomatic: Pian He volunteered through Zhai Tong and hammered a northern wing band for two thousand kills.

sentences.zh: 其後偏何連歲出兵擊北虜，還輒持首級詣遼東受賞賜。

translations.literal: Pian He then campaigned annually against the north and carried severed heads to Liaodong to collect reward.
translations.idiomatic: Year after year Pian He raided northward and cashed heads for Han silver at Liaodong.

sentences.zh: 三十年，鮮卑大人於仇賁、滿頭等率種人詣闕朝賀，慕義內屬。

translations.literal: In the thirtieth Jianwu year Xianbei leaders Yu Qiuben and Mantou led their peoples to court in homage and asked to dwell within the frontier.
translations.idiomatic: Jianwu 54: Yu Qiuben and Mantou brought their clans to Luoyang, eager to live under Han protection.

sentences.zh: 帝封於仇賁為王，滿頭為侯。

translations.literal: The emperor enfeoffed Yu Qiuben as king and Mantou as marquis.
translations.idiomatic: The court made Yu Qiuben a king and Mantou a marquis.

sentences.zh: 時漁陽赤山烏桓歆志賁等數寇上谷。

translations.literal: At that time the Chishan Wuhuan of Yuyang under Xin Zhiben repeatedly raided Shanggu.
translations.idiomatic: Yuyang’s Chishan Wuhuan, led by Xin Zhiben, kept hitting Shanggu.

sentences.zh: 永平元年，祭肜復賂偏何擊歆志賁，破斬之，於是鮮卑大人皆來歸附，並詣遼東受賞賜，青徐二州給錢歲二億七千萬為常。

translations.literal: In the first Yongping year Zhai Tong again bribed Pian He to attack Xin Zhiben, killed him, and thereafter every Xianbei chief came in; all went to Liaodong for reward, while Qing and Xu commanderies paid a fixed two hundred seventy million cash a year.
translations.idiomatic: Yongping 58: Zhai Tong paid Pian He to decapitate Xin Zhiben. Xianbei chiefs flocked to allegiance, collected stipends in Liaodong, and two inner provinces sent two hundred seventy million coins yearly to fund them.

sentences.zh: 明章二世，保塞無事。

translations.literal: Across Emperors Ming and Zhang the frontier stayed quiet.
translations.idiomatic: Emperors Ming and Zhang saw no major alarms on the wall.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 肥如縣，故城在今平州也。

translations.literal: [1] Feiru County’s old town lies in modern Pingzhou.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Ancient Feiru stood where Pingzhou later stood.

sentences.zh: 安帝永初中，鮮卑大人燕荔陽詣闕朝賀，鄧太后賜燕荔陽王印綬，赤車參駕，令止烏桓校尉所居甯城下，通胡市，因築南北兩部質館。

translations.literal: Early in Emperor An’s Yongchu era Xianbei chief Yan Liyang came to court; Empress Dowager Deng invested him with princely seals, crimson chariot with three horses, ordered him to halt beneath Ningcheng where the Wuhuan colonel lived, opened Hu markets, and built north and south hostage lodges.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor An’s widow welcomed Yan Liyang with kingly regalia, parked him under Ningcheng beside the colonel’s seat, licensed barbarian trade, and erected paired hostage compounds.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕鮮卑邑落百二十部，各遣入質。

translations.literal: [1] One hundred twenty Xianbei settlements each sent hostages.
translations.idiomatic: [1] All hundred-twenty Xianbei camps contributed noble sons as pledges.

sentences.zh: 是後或降或畔，與匈奴、烏桓更相攻擊。

translations.literal: Afterward they sometimes surrendered and sometimes rebelled, alternatively striking Han, Xiongnu, or Wuhuan.
translations.idiomatic: They swung between alliance and raid, trading blows with Han, Xiongnu, and Wuhuan by turns.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 築館以受降質。

translations.literal: [1] They raised lodges to house surrendered hostages.
translations.idiomatic: [1] The lodges housed surrendered barbarian pledges.

sentences.zh: 元初二年秋，遼東鮮卑圍無慮縣，〔一〕州郡合兵固保清野，鮮卑無所得。

translations.literal: In the autumn of the second Yuanchu year Liaodong Xianbei besieged Wulu county [1]; province and commandery pooled troops for scorched-earth defense so the Xianbei gained nothing.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanchu 115: Liaodong riders surrounded Wulu [1]; Han evacuated granaries and herds so the raiders starved.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕復攻扶黎營，殺長吏。

translations.literal: [2] They attacked Fuli camp again and killed senior officers.
translations.idiomatic: [2] They struck Fuli encampment and murdered command staff.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕四年，遼西鮮卑連休等遂燒塞門，寇百姓。

translations.literal: [3] In the fourth year Liaoxi Xianbei under Lianxiu burned gate towers and plundered settlers.
translations.idiomatic: [3] Yuanchu 117: Lianxiu’s Liaodong band fired frontier gates and looted farms.

sentences.zh: 烏桓大人於秩居等與連休有宿怨，共郡兵奔擊，大破之，斬首千三百級，悉獲其生口牛馬財物。

translations.literal: The Wuhuan leader Yu Zhiju bore old grudges against Lianxiu; he rode with commandery troops, smashed them, took thirteen hundred heads, and seized captives, cattle, horses, and goods.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Zhiju’s Wuhuan hated Lianxiu; allied county troops routed the raiders, claiming thirteen hundred skulls and heavy spoils.

sentences.zh: 五年秋，代郡鮮卑萬餘騎遂穿塞入寇，分攻城邑，燒官寺，殺長吏而去。

translations.literal: The next autumn more than ten thousand Dai commandery Xianbei punched through the wall, stormed towns, torched yamen, killed officers, and withdrew.
translations.idiomatic: Year six autumn: ten thousand Dai riders burst inward, torched offices, slew magistrates, and vanished.

sentences.zh: 乃發緣邊甲卒、黎陽營兵，屯上谷以備之。

translations.literal: Han drafted frontier armorers and Liyang-garrison troops and stationed them in Shanggu as a shield.
translations.idiomatic: Court summoned frontier levies and Liyang regulars to brace Shanggu.

sentences.zh: 冬，鮮卑入上谷，攻居庸關，復發緣邊諸郡、黎陽營兵、積射士步騎二萬人，屯列衝要。

translations.literal: That winter Xianbei entered Shanggu and struck Juyong Pass; Han again mobilized frontier commands, Liyang troops, and twenty thousand mixed shooters and cavalry to hold the chokepoints.
translations.idiomatic: Winter raids hit Juyong; Han stacked twenty thousand mounted archers along the passes.

sentences.zh: 六年秋，鮮卑入馬城塞，殺長吏，〔四〕度遼將軍鄧遵發積射士三千人，及中郎將馬續率南單于，與遼西、右北平兵馬會，出塞追擊鮮卑，大破之，獲生口及牛羊財物甚眾。

translations.literal: Next autumn they penetrated Macheng frontier [4]; General Who Crosses the Liao Deng Zun sent three thousand crack archers while Chief Commander Ma Xu led the Southern Chanyu and Liaoxi and Youbeiping columns beyond the wall, shattered the Xianbei, and seized many captives with herds and gear.
translations.idiomatic: Macheng fell under assault [4]; Deng Zun’s archers and Ma Xu’s allied army chased them out and packed off slaves and livestock.

sentences.zh: 又發積射士三千人，馬三千匹，詣度遼營屯守。

translations.literal: Three thousand more crack archers and three thousand horses marched to the Liao garrison for permanent duty.
translations.idiomatic: Another three thousand bowmen and mounts reinforced the Liao command permanently.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 無慮縣屬遼東郡。

translations.literal: [1] Wulu County belonged to Liaodong commandery.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Wulu sat inside Liaodong commandery.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 清野謂收斂積聚，不令寇得之也。

translations.literal: [2] “Clear fields” meant hauling stores indoors so raiders found nothing.
translations.idiomatic: [2] “Clearing fields” meant stripping the countryside bare ahead of the enemy.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 扶黎，縣，屬遼東屬國，故城在今營州東〔南〕。

translations.literal: [3] Fuli County in Liaodong dependent state—the ruins lie southeast of modern Yingzhou.
translations.idiomatic: [3] Fuli’s ruins stood southeast of Tang Yingzhou in the dependent Liaodong circuit.

sentences.zh: 〔四〕 馬城，縣名，屬代郡也。

translations.literal: [4] Macheng County belonged to Dai commandery.
translations.idiomatic: [4] Macheng County lay in Dai commandery.

sentences.zh: 永寧元年，遼西鮮卑大人烏倫、其至鞬率眾詣鄧遵降，奉貢獻。

translations.literal: In the first Yongning year Liaoxi Xianbei leaders Wulun and Qizhijian brought their people to surrender to Deng Zun with tribute.
translations.idiomatic: Yongning 120: Wulun and Qizhijian of Liaoxi presented Deng Zun their surrender and gifts.

sentences.zh: 詔封烏倫為率眾王，其至鞬為率眾侯，賜綵繒各有差。

translations.literal: An edict invested Wulun as prince who commands the masses and Qizhijian as marquis who commands the masses, awarding colored silks by rank.
translations.idiomatic: They received kingly and marquis titles “who commands the masses” plus graded silk allotments.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 縣名，屬五原郡也。

translations.literal: [1] That county name sits in Wuyuan commandery.
translations.idiomatic: [1] The gloss refers to a Wuyuan county of the same name.

sentences.zh: 順帝永建元年秋，鮮卑其至鞬寇代郡，太守李超戰死。

translations.literal: In the autumn of Emperor Shun’s first Yongjian year Xianbei Qizhijian raided Dai commandery and grand warden Li Chao died fighting.
translations.idiomatic: Yongjian 126 autumn: Qizhijian killed Li Chao defending Dai.

sentences.zh: 明年春，中郎將張國遣從事將南單于兵步騎萬餘人出塞，擊破之，獲其資重二千餘種。

translations.literal: Next spring Chief Commander Zhang Guo led Southern Xiongnu infantry and cavalry over ten thousand beyond the wall, routed them, and captured more than two thousand loads of baggage.
translations.idiomatic: The following spring Zhang Guo crossed the frontier with ten thousand allied riders and took two thousand wagonloads of loot.

sentences.zh: 時遼東鮮卑六千餘騎亦寇遼東玄菟，烏桓校尉耿曄發緣邊諸郡兵及烏桓率眾王出塞擊之，斬首數百級，大獲其生口牛馬什物，鮮卑乃率種眾三萬人詣遼東乞降。

translations.literal: Meanwhile six thousand Liaodong raiders struck Liaodong and Xuantu; Colonel Geng Ye summoned frontier militias and Wuhuan prince-commanders, chased them out, took hundreds of heads, seized livestock and baggage, and thirty thousand Xianbei came to Liaodong begging surrender.
translations.idiomatic: Six thousand Liaodong riders hit Xuantu until Geng Ye’s frontier coalition butchered them and captured herds; thirty thousand Xianbei later sued for peace at Liaodong.

sentences.zh: 三年，四年，鮮卑頻寇漁陽、朔方。

translations.literal: In the third and fourth years Xianbei repeatedly raided Yuyang and Shuofang.
translations.idiomatic: Years three and four brought repeated strikes on Yuyang and Shuofang.

sentences.zh: 六年秋，耿曄遣司馬將胡兵數千人，出塞擊破之。

translations.literal: That autumn Geng Ye sent a major with thousands of barbarian troops beyond the wall and broke them.
translations.idiomatic: Autumn counterstrike: Geng Ye’s major-led barbarian column smashed them outside the wall.

sentences.zh: 冬，漁陽太守又遣烏桓兵擊之，斬首八百級，獲牛馬生口。

translations.literal: Winter: Yuyang grand warden sent Wuhuan auxiliaries who took eight hundred heads plus cattle, horses, and captives.
translations.idiomatic: Winter raids ended when Yuyang’s Wuhuan allies stacked eight hundred skulls and drove back herds.

sentences.zh: 烏桓豪人扶漱官勇健，〔一〕每與鮮卑戰，輒陷敵，詔賜號「率眾君」。

translations.literal: The Wuhuan stalwart Fushu Guan was fearless [1]; each clash with Xianbei saw him pierce the enemy line, so the court dubbed him “Prince who Commands the Masses.”
translations.idiomatic: [1] Fushu Guan (“shu” read suo-jiu fan) spearheaded every fight against Xianbei until Han titled him “Prince who Commands the Masses.”

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 漱音所救反。

translations.literal: [1] Shu is read suo-jiu fan.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Graph “shu” follows suo-jiu fanqie.

sentences.zh: 陽嘉元年冬，耿曄遣烏桓親漢都尉戎朱廆率眾王侯咄歸等，出塞抄擊鮮卑，大斬獲而還，賜咄歸等已下為率眾王、侯、長，賜綵繒各有差。

translations.literal: Winter of Yangjia year one: Geng Ye dispatched Wuhuan Colonel-close-to-Han Rong Zhuwei with prince-dukes Zhu Gui beyond the wall to rip through Xianbei; rewards raised Zhu Gui and others to prince, marquis, and elder ranks with graded silks.
translations.idiomatic: Yangjia 132 winter: Rong Zhuwei’s raid yielded heavy trophies; emperor promoted Zhu Gui’s party with silk bales.

sentences.zh: 鮮卑後寇遼東屬國，於是耿曄乃移屯遼東無慮城拒之。

translations.literal: When Xianbei struck Liaodong dependent state afterward, Geng Ye shifted his headquarters to Wulu city in Liaodong to block them.
translations.idiomatic: Renewed Liaodong raids forced Geng Ye to relocate his garrison to frontier Wulu.

sentences.zh: 二年春，匈奴中郎將趙稠遣從事將南匈奴骨都侯夫沈等，出塞擊鮮卑，破之，斬獲甚眾，詔賜夫沈金印紫綬及縑綵各有差。

translations.literal: Spring year two: Chief Commander of the Xiongnu Zhao Chou sent aides leading Southern Xiongnu Gutu nobles such as Fuchen beyond the wall; they routed Xianbei; Fuchen earned gold seal on purple ribbon plus silk.
translations.idiomatic: Southern Gutu officer Fuchen won purple-seal honors after Zhao Chou’s spring expedition shattered another wave.

sentences.zh: 秋，鮮卑穿塞入馬城，代郡太守擊之，不能克。

translations.literal: That autumn Xianbei bored through the wall into Macheng; Dai grand warden attacked without winning.
translations.idiomatic: They punched Macheng again that autumn; local Han troops failed to expel them.

sentences.zh: 後其至鞬死，鮮卑抄盜差稀。

translations.literal: After Qizhijian died, Xianbei banditry grew comparatively scarce.
translations.idiomatic: Once Qizhijian was gone the raids thinned out.

sentences.zh: 桓帝時，鮮卑檀石槐者，其父投鹿侯、初從匈奴軍三年，其妻在家生子。

translations.literal: Under Emperor Huan lived Tanshi Huai of the Xianbei; his father Touluhou had spent three years with a Xiongnu army while his wife bore a son at home.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Huan’s era produced Tanshi Huai; father Touluhou was abroad three campaigns while the baby arrived.

sentences.zh: 投鹿侯歸，怪欲殺之。

translations.literal: When Touluhou returned he thought it monstrous and meant to kill the child.
translations.idiomatic: Touluhou returned furious and reached for his sword.

sentences.zh: 妻言嘗晝行聞雷震，仰天視而雹入其口，因吞之，遂妊身，十月而產，此子必有奇異，且宜長視。

translations.literal: His wife said she had walked by day, heard thunder, looked skyward as hail flew into her mouth, swallowed it, conceived, and bore him after ten months—surely the boy would be extraordinary and deserved rearing.
translations.idiomatic: She pleaded a thunder-and-hail miracle pregnancy and begged him to spare this destined prodigy.

sentences.zh: 投鹿侯不聽，遂棄之。

translations.literal: Touluhou ignored her and abandoned the infant.
translations.idiomatic: He refused and cast the baby out.

sentences.zh: 妻私語家令收養焉，名檀石槐。

translations.literal: She secretly told neighbors to raise him and named him Tanshi Huai.
translations.idiomatic: Kin hid the boy and named him Tanshi Huai.

sentences.zh: 年十四五，勇健有智略。

translations.literal: At fourteen or fifteen he was brave, vigorous, and clever.
translations.idiomatic: By mid-teens he was already fearless and cunning.

sentences.zh: 異部大人抄取其外家牛羊，檀石槐單騎追擊之，所向無前，悉還得所亡者，由是部落畏服。

translations.literal: When another tribe’s chief stole his maternal kin’s cattle and sheep, Tanshi Huai rode alone in pursuit, smashed every foe ahead, recovered everything lost, and won awe throughout the camps.
translations.idiomatic: A rival chief rustled his uncle’s herd; Huai charged solo, scattered them, won every beast back, and earned universal dread.

sentences.zh: 乃施法禁，平曲直，無敢犯者，遂推以為大人。

translations.literal: He imposed laws and settled grievances; none dared violate him, so they elevated him as great man.
translations.idiomatic: He legislated disputes away until camps hailed him chieftain.

sentences.zh: 檀石槐乃立庭於彈汗山歠仇水上，〔一〕去高柳北三百餘里，兵馬甚盛，東西部大人皆歸焉。

translations.literal: He pitched his court on Mount Tanhan beside the Chuchou River [1], over three hundred li north of Gaoliu, mustered huge armies, and drew eastern and western chiefs to his banner.
translations.idiomatic: His headquarters sat north of Gaoliu on Tanhan by Chuchou water [1]; hosts gathered until both wings obeyed.

sentences.zh: 因南抄緣邊，北拒丁零，東卻夫餘，西擊烏孫，盡據匈奴故地，東西萬四千餘里，南北七千餘里，網羅山川水澤鹽池。

translations.literal: He raided south along the frontier, held Dingling at bay in the north, pushed Fuyu eastward, struck Wusun westward, seized the old Xiongnu heartland, stretched fourteen thousand li east-west and seven thousand li north-south, and netted mountains, rivers, and salt pans.
translations.idiomatic: He burned the frontier belt, boxed Dingling, routed Fuyu, bruised Wusun, reclaimed Xiongnu pastures fourteen thousand li wide and seven thousand deep—salt flats and rivers included.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 歠音昌悅反。

translations.literal: [1] Chuo is read chang-yue fan.
translations.idiomatic: [1] “Chuo” takes chang-yue fanqie.

sentences.zh: 永壽二年秋，檀石槐遂將三四千騎寇雲中。

translations.literal: In the autumn of the second Yongshou year Tanshi Huai led three or four thousand riders against Yunzhong.
translations.idiomatic: Yongshou 156 autumn: Huai struck Yunzhong with a few thousand riders.

sentences.zh: 延熹元年，鮮卑寇北邊。

translations.literal: In the first Yanxi year the Xianbei raided the northern marches.
translations.idiomatic: Yanxi 158 opened with Xianbei strikes along the northern frontier.

sentences.zh: 冬，使匈奴中郎將張奐率南單于出塞擊之，斬首二百級。

translations.literal: That winter the court ordered Chief Commander of the Xiongnu Zhang Huan to lead the Southern Chanyu beyond the wall; they took two hundred heads.
translations.idiomatic: Winter: Zhang Huan and the Southern Chanyu rode out and stacked two hundred Xianbei skulls.

sentences.zh: 二年，復入鴈門，殺數百人，大抄掠而去。

translations.literal: The next year they entered Yanmen again, killed several hundred, looted heavily, and withdrew.
translations.idiomatic: Year two they flooded Yanmen, massacred hundreds, and vanished with booty.

sentences.zh: 六年夏，千餘騎寇遼東屬國。

translations.literal: In the summer of the sixth year more than a thousand riders struck Liaodong dependent state.
translations.idiomatic: Summer year six: a thousand riders hit the Liaodong frontier circuit.

sentences.zh: 九年夏，遂分騎數萬人入緣邊九郡，並殺掠吏人，於是復遣張奐擊之，鮮卑乃出塞去。

translations.literal: In the summer of the ninth year they split tens of thousands of horsemen across nine frontier commanderies, killing and plundering officials and commoners alike; the court again dispatched Zhang Huan, and the Xianbei fled beyond the passes.
translations.idiomatic: Yanxi 166 summer: wave riders tore through nine border prefectures until Zhang Huan chased them back across the frontier.

sentences.zh: 朝廷積患之，而不能制，遂遣使持印綬封檀石槐為王，欲與和親。

translations.literal: The court nursed this grievance yet could not subdue them, so envoys carried seals to invest Tanshi Huai as king in hopes of marriage alliance.
translations.idiomatic: Luoyang admitted helplessness and offered Huai a royal patent and peace ties.

sentences.zh: 檀石槐不肯受，而寇抄滋甚。

translations.literal: Tanshi Huai refused the honor while raids only grew worse.
translations.idiomatic: Huai spurned the title and doubled the violence.

sentences.zh: 乃自分其地為三部，從右北平以東至遼東，接夫餘、濊貊二十餘邑為東部，從右北平以西至上谷十餘邑為中部，從上谷以西至敦煌、烏孫二十餘邑為西部，各置大人主領之，皆屬檀石槐。

translations.literal: He then carved his realm into three divisions: from Youbeiping east to Liaodong, touching Fuyu and Huimo across twenty-odd settlements, formed the east; from Youbeiping west to Shanggu, ten-odd settlements, the middle; from Shanggu west to Dunhuang and Wusun, twenty-odd settlements, the west—each division had its own great man answering to Tanshi Huai.
translations.idiomatic: He triangulated the steppe—eastern wing against Fuyu, central corridor above Shanggu, western wing reaching Dunhuang—each wing commanded by a deputy under Huai himself.

sentences.zh: 靈帝立，幽、并、涼三州緣邊諸郡無歲不被鮮卑寇抄，殺略不可勝數。

translations.literal: After Emperor Ling ascended, not a year passed without Xianbei raids along You, Bing, and Liang—the casualties beyond counting.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ling inherited endless Xianbei devastation across Youzhou, Bingzhou, and Liangzhou.

sentences.zh: 熹平三年冬，鮮卑入北地，太守夏育率休著屠各追擊破之。

translations.literal: Winter of the third Xiping year Xianbei entered Beidi; grand warden Xia Yu led Xiuzhu Tuge auxiliaries in pursuit and broke them.
translations.idiomatic: Xiping 174 winter: Xia Yu’s Tuge riders chased Xianbei out of Beidi commandery.

sentences.zh: 遷育為護烏桓校尉。

translations.literal: Yu was promoted to Colonel Protecting the Wuhuan.
translations.idiomatic: The court moved Xia Yu into the Wuhuan colonel’s chair.

sentences.zh: 五年，鮮卑寇幽州。

translations.literal: In the fifth year the Xianbei raided Youzhou.
translations.idiomatic: Year five brought another Youzhou incursion.

sentences.zh: 六年夏，鮮卑寇三邊。

translations.literal: In the sixth summer they struck three frontier belts at once.
translations.idiomatic: Summer six: simultaneous raids on three sectors of the wall.

sentences.zh: 秋，夏育上言：「鮮卑寇邊，自春以來，三十餘發，請徵幽州諸郡兵出塞擊之，一冬二春，必能禽滅。

translations.literal: That autumn Xia Yu submitted: “Since spring the Xianbei have hit us over thirty times; I ask to mobilize every Youzhou command beyond the wall—for one winter and two springs we can capture and destroy them.
translations.idiomatic: Autumn memorial: Xia Yu counted thirty spring-to-date raids and demanded a winter-plus-two-spring eradication campaign from Youzhou.

sentences.zh: 」朝廷未許。

translations.literal: ” The court did not approve.
translations.idiomatic: The throne withheld consent.

sentences.zh: 先是護羌校尉田晏坐事論刑被原，欲立功自效，乃請中常侍王甫求得為將，甫因此議遣兵與育并力討賊。

translations.literal: Earlier Colonel Protecting the Qiang Tian Yan had been sentenced for an offense yet pardoned; hungering to redeem himself he bribed eunuch Wang Fu for a command; Fu then urged deploying troops to aid Yu against the bandits.
translations.idiomatic: Disgraced Colonel Tian Yan bought a generalship through Wang Fu and lobbied for a joint strike with Xia Yu.

sentences.zh: 帝乃拜晏為破鮮卑中郎將。

translations.literal: The emperor therefore commissioned Yan as chief commander for crushing the Xianbei.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ling named Tian Yan “Chief Commander against the Xianbei.”

sentences.zh: 大臣多有不同，乃召百官議朝堂。

translations.literal: Senior ministers split; he summoned the hundred officials to debate in the palace hall.
translations.idiomatic: Dissent in council forced an open court debate.

sentences.zh: 議郎蔡邕議曰：

translations.literal: Gentleman Consultant Cai Yong argued:
translations.idiomatic: Cai Yong spoke for the conservatives:

sentences.zh: 書戒猾夏，易伐鬼方，〔一〕周有獫狁、蠻荊之師，〔二〕漢有闐顏、瀚海之事。

translations.literal: The Documents caution how barbarians disturb the Xia lands; the Changes praises striking Gui Fang; note one explains those lines. Zhou raised armies against the Xianyun and the Manjing; note two cites that ode. Han fought through Mount Tianyan and the Han Sea.
translations.idiomatic: Cai Yong piled precedent: the Shang shu and Zhou yi warn of frontier foes; Zhou battled Xianyun and southern tribes; Han echoed that reach from Tianyan to the northern sea.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕征討殊類，所由尚矣。

translations.literal: Note three: campaigning against alien peoples has honored precedent since antiquity.
translations.idiomatic: Punishing foreign foes, he argued, was an ancient constant.

sentences.zh: 然而時有同異，埶有可否，故謀有得失，事有成敗，不可齊也。

translations.literal: Yet times differ, circumstances allow or forbid, so plans win or fail and outcomes cannot be forced uniform.
translations.idiomatic: What worked once may fail now; strategy must follow the moment.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 尚書舜典曰：「蠻夷猾夏，寇賊姦宄。

translations.literal: Note one: the Shun dian of the Shang shu says: “Barbarians make trouble in the Hua lands, raiders and traitors work mischief.”
translations.idiomatic: The Shun dian brands border peoples who stir the interior as raiders.

sentences.zh: 」猾，亂也。

translations.literal: ” Hua means “to throw into disorder.”
translations.idiomatic: “Hua” in that line means to disorder.

sentences.zh: 易既濟九三爻辭曰：「高宗伐鬼方，三年而克之。

translations.literal: The Jiji hexagram, third line, reads: “Gaozong campaigned against Gui Fang; after three years he overcame it.”
translations.idiomatic: The Zhou yi celebrates a three-year Shang war on Gui Fang.

sentences.zh: 」前書淮南王安曰：「鬼方，小蠻夷也。

translations.literal: ” The Prince of Huainan in the Former Han shu said: “Gui Fang was a petty barbarian people.”
translations.idiomatic: Liu An called Gui Fang a minor tribe.

sentences.zh: 」音義曰：「鬼方，遠方也。」

translations.literal: ” The pronunciations gloss adds: “Gui Fang means a distant land.”
translations.idiomatic: Commentators gloss Gui Fang simply as the far marches.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 詩小雅曰：「顯允方叔，征伐獫狁，蠻荊來威。」

translations.literal: Note two: the Odes’ “Minor Odes” has: “Illustrious Fang Shu campaigned against the Xianyun; the Manjing came to fear his might.”
translations.idiomatic: The Odes tie Fang Shu’s Xianyun war to aweing the south.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 武帝使大將軍衛青擊匈奴，至闐顏山，斬首萬餘級。

translations.literal: Note three: Emperor Wu sent Grand General Wei Qing against the Xiongnu to Mount Tianyan, taking more than ten thousand heads.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu’s Wei Qing reached Tianyan with ten thousand kills.

sentences.zh: 使霍去病擊匈奴，封狼居胥山，登臨瀚海也。

translations.literal: He sent Huo Qubing to strike the Xiongnu, enfeoffing him on Mount Langjuxu and bringing him to overlook the Hanhai.
translations.idiomatic: Huo Qubing sealed Mount Langjuxu and gazed on the great northern sea.

sentences.zh: 武帝情存遠略，志闢四方，南誅百越，北討強胡，西伐大宛，東并朝鮮。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu’s heart was set on distant plans; he meant to open the four quarters—punishing the Hundred Yue in the south, the mighty Hu in the north, campaigning against Dayuan in the west, and annexing Joseon in the east.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu pursued glory on every frontier—south against the Yue, north against the Xiongnu, west against Dayuan, east against Korea.

sentences.zh: 因文、景之蓄，藉天下之饒，數十年閒，官民俱匱。

translations.literal: Riding the treasuries left by Emperors Wen and Jing and the realm’s plenty, within a few decades both government and people were exhausted.
translations.idiomatic: He spent down the Wen-Jing surplus until court and countryside were broke.

sentences.zh: 乃興鹽鐵酒榷之利，設告緡重稅之令，〔一〕民不堪命，起為盜賊，關東紛擾，道路不通。

translations.literal: He then profited from salt, iron, and wine monopolies and issued the heavy suanmin tax and informer laws; note one the people could not endure the edicts and rose as bandits; east of the passes convulsed and roads closed.
translations.idiomatic: Monopolies on salt, iron, and wine plus the suanmin surcharges note one drove commoners to revolt and cut the roads east of Hangu.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕繡衣直指之使，奮鈇鉞而並出。

translations.literal: Note two robed straight-batons envoys brandished axes and fanned out together.
translations.idiomatic: Next came the embroidered-robes commissioners with axes note two.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕既而覺悟，乃息兵罷役，〔封〕丞相為富人侯。

translations.literal: Note three when he awoke to the damage he stilled armies and ended corvée and enfeoffed the chancellor as Marquis of the Rich; textual gloss variant inserts “enfeoff.”
translations.idiomatic: Only later did he demobilize and reward his chancellor as “rich marquis” to signal recovery note three.

sentences.zh: 〔四〕故主父偃曰：「夫務戰勝，窮武事，未有不悔者也。

translations.literal: Note four hence Zhufu Yan said, “He who chases total victory in war and exhausts the military will always regret it.”
translations.idiomatic: Zhufu Yan warned that wars of annihilation breed regret note four.

sentences.zh: 」〔五〕夫以世宗神武，將相良猛，財賦充實，所拓廣遠，猶有悔焉。

translations.literal: ” Note five even with Shizong’s divine soldiery, able generals, and full treasuries, the expansion was vast and he still had regrets.
translations.idiomatic: Note five: even Emperor Wu’s elite armies and bursting granaries could not banish second thoughts.

sentences.zh: 況今人財並乏，事劣昔時乎！

translations.literal: How much more when our people and wealth are both wanting and the enterprise is feebler than of old!
translations.idiomatic: Today we are poorer and weaker than his age.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 武帝使東郭咸陽等領天下鹽鐵，敢私鑄錢賣鹽者釱左趾。

translations.literal: Note one: Emperor Wu set Dongguo Xianyang and others over the empire’s salt and iron; private coining or salt sales meant fetters on the left foot.
translations.idiomatic: State monopolies note one riveted smugglers’ ankles.

sentences.zh: 榷，專也。

translations.literal: Que means “exclusive.”
translations.idiomatic: “Monopoly” (que) means exclusive sales.

sentences.zh: 官自賣酒，人不得賣也。

translations.literal: The government sold wine; commoners could not peddle it.
translations.idiomatic: Imperial cellars held the retail license.

sentences.zh: 又筭緡錢，率緡錢二千而筭一，令各以其物自占。

translations.literal: He also assessed min-cash, roughly one suan per two thousand cash, ordering each to declare his property.
translations.idiomatic: The suanmin tax took one cut per two thousand cash of declared wealth.

sentences.zh: 占不悉，聽人告緡，以半與之。

translations.literal: If declarations were incomplete, others could denounce for half the fine.
translations.idiomatic: Denouncers split forfeitures with the treasury.

sentences.zh: 音義曰：「緡，絲也。

translations.literal: The pronunciation gloss says: “Min is silk.
translations.idiomatic: Gloss: min originally meant silk cord.

sentences.zh: 用以貫錢，故曰緡錢。

translations.literal: Used to string coins, hence min-cash.”
translations.idiomatic: Strings of coins were counted by those cords.

sentences.zh: 一筭百二十也。」

translations.literal: Each suan equaled one hundred twenty cash.”
translations.idiomatic: Each assessment unit meant one hundred twenty copper coins.”

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 武帝天漢二年，泰山、琅邪群賊徐勃等阻山攻城，道路不通。

translations.literal: Note two: Tianhan second year Mount Tai and Langye bandits under Xu Bo seized mountains and stormed towns until roads closed.
translations.idiomatic: Bandits note two cut communications through Taishan in 99 BCE.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 武帝使直指使者暴勝之等衣繡仗斧，分部逐捕也。

translations.literal: Note three: Emperor Wu sent straight-arrow envoys such as Bao Shengzhi in embroidered robes with axes to hunt rebels by sector.
translations.idiomatic: Straight-arrow commissioners note three carried axe authority district by district.

sentences.zh: 〔四〕 封丞相車千秋為富人侯，以明休息，思富養人。

translations.literal: Note four: he enfeoffed Chancellor Che Qianqiu as Marquis of the Rich to show rest and intent to enrich and nurture the people.
translations.idiomatic: Che Qianqiu’s “rich marquis” patent signaled retreat note four.

sentences.zh: 〔五〕 武帝時，齊相主父偃諫伐匈奴之辭。

translations.literal: Note five: reproof from Qi Chancellor Zhufu Yan against attacking the Xiongnu during Emperor Wu’s reign.
translations.idiomatic: Zhufu Yan’s anti-Hun memorial note five closes the parallel.

sentences.zh: 自匈奴遁逃，鮮卑強盛，據其故地，稱兵十萬，才力勁健，意智益生。

translations.literal: After the Xiongnu fled, the Xianbei grew strong, held their old lands, mustered a hundred thousand spears, and grew ever tougher and wilier.
translations.idiomatic: Xiongnu collapse let the Xianbei fill the steppe with a hundred thousand alert riders.

sentences.zh: 加以關塞不嚴，禁網多漏，精金良鐵，皆為賊有；

translations.literal: Add loose passes and leaking prohibitions: fine gold and good iron all fell to the raiders.
translations.idiomatic: Lax border controls smuggled Han steel into nomad hands.

sentences.zh: 漢人逋逃，為之謀主，兵利馬疾，過於匈奴。

translations.literal: Han fugitives became their strategists; sharp weapons and swift horses made them more dangerous than the Xiongnu.
translations.idiomatic: Defecting Chinese advisers and better mounts outclassed the old Xiongnu threat.

sentences.zh: 昔段熲良將，習兵善戰，有事西羌，猶十餘年。

translations.literal: Duan Jiong was a tested commander adept at war; his western Qiang campaigns still lasted ten-plus years.
translations.idiomatic: Even Duan Jiong needed a decade to tame Qiang rebels.

sentences.zh: 今育、晏才策，未必過熲，鮮卑種眾，不弱于曩時。

translations.literal: Yu and Yan’s talents need not surpass Jiong’s, yet the Xianbei masses are no weaker than before.
translations.idiomatic: Xia Yu and Tian Yan are hardly superior generals, while Xianbei strength matches earlier highs.

sentences.zh: 而虛計二載，自許有成，若禍結兵連，豈得中休？

translations.literal: Their airy promise of victory inside two years—if disaster chains battle after battle, can we halt midway?
translations.idiomatic: Promising a two-year wipeout invites an endless quagmire.

sentences.zh: 當復徵發眾人，轉運無已，是為耗竭諸夏，并力蠻夷。

translations.literal: That means mobilizing the multitude again and shuttling supplies without end—draining the Central Plain to fuel barbarians.
translations.idiomatic: Further drafts would beggar north China to enrich the steppe.

sentences.zh: 夫邊垂之患，手足之蚧搔；

translations.literal: Frontier peril is an itch on hand or foot;
translations.idiomatic: Border raids are irritants—

sentences.zh: 中國之困，胸背之瘭疽。

translations.literal: internal distress is a gangrenous sore on chest or back.
translations.idiomatic: but domestic collapse is a mortal abscess at the heart.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕方今郡縣盜賊尚不能禁，況此醜虜而可伏乎！

translations.literal: Commentary mark one: today we cannot even suppress county bandits—could we truly crush these ugly barbarians?
translations.idiomatic: Commentary note one: if the capital cannot stifle banditry in its own counties, how can it subjugate these steppe hosts?

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 蚧音介。

translations.literal: Commentary mark one: jie is read jie.
translations.idiomatic: Gloss: jie sounds like “jie.”

sentences.zh: 搔音新到反。

translations.literal: Sao is read xin-dao fan.
translations.idiomatic: “Scratch” (sao) uses xin-dao fanqie.

sentences.zh: 埤蒼曰：「瘭音必燒反。

translations.literal: The Picao says: “biao is read bi-shao fan.
translations.idiomatic: The Picao glossary gives bi-shao for biao.

sentences.zh: 」杜預注左傳曰：「疽，惡創也。」

translations.literal: ” Du Yu’s Zuo commentary gloss: “Ju is a malignant sore.”
translations.idiomatic: Du Yu defines ju as a malignant ulcer.

sentences.zh: 昔高祖忍平城之恥，呂后棄慢書之詬，〔一〕方之於今，何者為甚？

translations.literal: Gaozu endured the Pingcheng shame and Empress Lü swallowed the insult of the arrogant letter commentary mark one—which compares worse with today?
translations.idiomatic: Han founders swallowed worse humiliations than we face—why panic now? commentary one refers to the insulting Xiongnu letter to Lü Zhi.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 詬，恥也，音許豆反。

translations.literal: Commentary mark one: gou means shame; read xu-dou fan.
translations.idiomatic: Gou means shame; pronunciation xu-dou fanqie.

sentences.zh: 天設山河，秦築長城，漢起塞垣，所以別內外，異殊俗也。

translations.literal: Heaven set mountains and rivers; Qin built the Long Wall; Han raised frontier ramparts to divide inner from outer and separate customs.
translations.idiomatic: Natural barriers plus Qin and Han walls marked civilization from steppe.

sentences.zh: 苟無䠞國內侮之患則可矣，〔一〕豈與蟲螘

translations.literal: If there were no calamity of mutiny against a weakened state it would suffice [1]; how could one still—
translations.idiomatic: Solve civil breakdown [1] and we might breathe—why keep—

translations.literal: Variant gloss inserted between graphs.
translations.idiomatic: Editors mark an alternate reading between the preceding characters.

sentences.zh: 〔狡〕寇計爭往來哉！

translations.literal: …vie endlessly over raids with crafty foes like worms?” Editorial gloss substitutes “crafty” into the preceding clause.
translations.idiomatic: …squander wit trading blows with gnats?” Commentators emend one graph to read “crafty.”

sentences.zh: 雖或破之，豈可殄盡，而方

translations.literal: Though sometimes defeating them, how could they be utterly wiped out—and textual variant reads “now” where others read…
translations.idiomatic: Occasional victories cannot exterminate them—and some editions read “now” where others read…

translations.literal: …“would,” editorial gloss variant.
translations.idiomatic: …“would,” following an editorial substitution for the next clause.

sentences.zh: 〔令〕本朝為之旰食乎？

translations.literal: …editorial gloss variant “order”—have our dynasty skip supper from anxiety?”
translations.idiomatic: …make this court dine after midnight from sheer dread?”

translations.literal: Commentary mark two.
translations.idiomatic: Commentary note two ends here.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 䠞國，解見西域傳。

translations.literal: Commentary mark one “crippled polity” gloss appears in the Western Regions treatise.
translations.idiomatic: The phrase “crippled polity” is glossed in the Xiyu zhuan.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 旰，晚也。

translations.literal: Commentary mark two gan means late.
translations.idiomatic: Gan means eating late into the night.

sentences.zh: 左傳伍子胥曰：「楚君大夫，其旰食乎！」

translations.literal: Wu Zixu in the Zuo zhuan said: “Chu’s lord and ministers—will they dine late?”
translations.idiomatic: Wu Zixu’s lament about Chu rulers eating dinner at midnight.

sentences.zh: 夫專勝者未必克，挾疑者未必敗，眾所謂危，聖人不任，朝議有嫌，明主不行也。

translations.literal: Obsession with victory does not assure triumph; doubt does not assure defeat; what the crowd calls peril sages will not stake on; policies court suspicion wise rulers avoid.
translations.idiomatic: Forced victories fail as often as hesitant gambits; wise rulers ignore panicky councils.

sentences.zh: 昔淮南王安諫伐越曰：「天子之兵，有征無戰。
